Reading Swing from a Lead Sheet

A lead sheet writes swing eighths as plain eighth notes, and that is not an error. The way they are written is shorthand, the way a chord symbol is. It tells you which notes come where, and the style tells you how to play them. This lesson covers what the shorthand means, how much room it leaves you, and how to know when it does not mean swing. The two examples are Oscar Pettiford’s Blues in the Closet, which swings, and Herbie Hancock’s Watermelon Man, which does not.

How to use the page. Every example is written out and can be played. Press ▶ Play to hear it. Examples that have a Swing slider let you set how long the first eighth of each pair is held, from even (50%) up to a dotted-eighth-and-sixteenth (75%). The Tempo box sets the speed. Play each example at more than one setting before you read on.

1. What the page says, and what it means

Here is the first bar of Blues in the Closet exactly as a lead sheet writes it.

Played as written, the eighths are even: each beat is split exactly in half. No jazz player reads it that way. In a swing tune each pair of eighths is played long-short: the note on the beat is held longer and the note on the “and” comes late. The usual way to explain it is with a triplet: the beat is split into three, the first note gets two thirds and the second gets one.

Arrangers almost never write that, because it is hard to read and because, as the rest of this lesson shows, it is not quite right either. Instead they write plain eighths and put a word or a sign at the top of the chart:

  • Swing, Med. swing, Shuffle, Bluesy, or just a tempo and a style name.
  • The sign ♫ = ♩ ♪³: “a pair of eighths equals a quarter and an eighth under a triplet”.
  • Nothing at all. On a jazz lead sheet, swing is the default, and you are expected to know it.

The one way not to read swing eighths is as a dotted eighth and a sixteenth. That is a ratio of 3 to 1, and at most tempos it sounds stiff and jerky, like a march. Compare it with the triplet version above.

2. Swing is a range, not a ratio

The triplet is a useful first picture and a poor final answer. Measurements of recordings find that players swing anywhere from nearly even to a little past the triplet, and that the same player changes ratio with the tempo. The rough rule:

Tempo Typical long:short Slider What it sounds like
Ballad, slow blues (under 80) about 2:1, sometimes more 65–70% Lazy, heavy triplet feel, often a 12/8 shuffle
Medium (100–160) between 3:2 and 2:1 60–67% The “standard” swing of a blues like Blues in the Closet
Up-tempo (over 220) close to even 52–58% Eighths almost straight; the swing is in the accents

The band on this site follows the same rule: its swing starts at 68% at 100 beats a minute and slides toward 60% as the tempo rises. Try it here. Set the slider to 66% and raise the tempo to 240: it becomes hard to play and starts to sound like a shuffle. Then lower the slider to 55% at the same tempo.

Everything else the shorthand leaves to you

The ratio is only one of the choices a plain line of eighths leaves open. Others matter at least as much, and the lead sheet says nothing about any of them.

  • Accents on the off-beats. Swing players lean on the “and”, not the beat. A line of eighths is usually played doo-BAH doo-BAH, with the beat note soft and the off-beat note pushed. This is why fast swing still swings at nearly even eighths.
  • Ghosted notes. A note in the middle of a run may be barely played at all, more felt than heard.
  • Length. A written quarter note is often played short (dit), especially on beats 2 and 4 and at the end of a phrase. A written eighth tied over the bar line is played long.
  • Where in the beat. Some players sit right on the beat, others play a fraction behind it (“laid back”) against a drummer who is on top of it. Neither is written; both are swing.
  • Small changes to the rhythm. Players anticipate a note by an eighth, delay one, or add a pickup. On a lead sheet, that is interpretation, not a wrong note.

What is not up to you: where the bar lines are, where the notes fall in the beat (on it or on the “and”), and the form. A swing eighth on the “and” of 2 is late, but it is still the “and” of 2.

3. Blues in the Closet

Blues in the Closet is a medium-tempo jazz blues, usually played somewhere between 120 and 180 beats a minute. Here is the whole melody, in F, as it is written in the tune library.

There is no “Swing” marking on it, and none is needed: it is a bebop-era blues, every recording of it swings, and the eighth-note pairs are written the way every jazz player expects. Play it at 50% and then at 64% to hear what the marking would have told you.

The places that change when it swings

  • The pickup and the ties. The tune starts on the “and” of 4 and ties it into the bar. In swing, that pickup is late (it is the short note of a pair), so the first note of the tune arrives just before the bar line and pulls the band into it. The same figure ends bars 4 and 8. These anticipations are the strongest swing feature in the tune: give them a little accent.
  • The figure A F. In every bar the melody drops from the 3rd to the root in a pair of eighths. Swung, it is long-short, and the short F is the one to lean on.
  • The tied F in bar 2. A/F/- F/ C is four eighths, with the second tied to the third. Swung, the tied F lands on the late “and” of 2 and sustains through beat 3. Played even, the syncopation is weaker and the bar sounds square.
  • The long notes. The C in bars 4 and 8 is a dotted quarter tied to a quarter. It can be held full length or cut off early; both are common. The rest that follows is where the rhythm section, or another player, answers.

A range of good readings

Three players reading the same lead sheet would not play the same thing, and all three would be right. Try these settings and decide which one you like:

Setting Tempo Slider Feel
Relaxed 120 66–68% Close to the triplet, heavy, bluesy
Medium 150 60–64% The usual jam-session reading
Up 200+ 55–58% Nearly even; put the swing in accents on the off-beats

What no setting allows is 50% at a medium tempo with every note accented equally. That is the one clear misreading.

4. Watermelon Man: eighths that do not swing

Watermelon Man (from Takin’ Off, 1962) is also a blues, with 16 bars instead of 12, and it is written in exactly the same way: plain eighth notes, no triplets, no dots. Here are its first eight bars and the four-bar riff that follows.

On the page it looks like Blues in the Closet: eighth notes, ties over the bar line, anticipations. The difference is the style. This is a straight-eighth tune: the eighths are even, and they stay even when the tempo drops. It is often marked “Funky”, “Latin”, “Even 8ths” or “Straight 8ths”, but on many lead sheets it is not marked at all, and you are expected to know it from the record, the same as with a swing tune.

Now move the slider to 66% and play it again. Bars 9 to 12 suffer most: z2 cc g2 a2 starts on an off-beat pair, and swinging it turns a crisp, funky riff into something closer to a nursery rhyme. The off-beat F in bars 2 and 6, which should snap against the beat, goes soft.

“Somewhere between”

Even this tune is not perfectly even. Hancock said that Billy Higgins played it “somewhere between straight eighth notes and the swinging triplets of jazz”. That is a slider setting of perhaps 53 to 56%, which is not enough to sound like swing but is enough to keep the line from sounding mechanical. Mongo Santamaría’s hit version a year later is a cha-cha, and its eighths are straight. Both are good readings of the same lead sheet; a 66% swing is not.

So the range of acceptable readings exists for straight tunes too. It is just centred in a different place.

5. The contrast, side by side

Blues in the Closet Watermelon Man
Written as Plain eighths Plain eighths
Played as Swing, long-short Even, or very nearly
Slider 55–68%, by tempo 50–56%
Where the energy is Accents on the off-beats, late pickups Crisp, equal subdivisions locked to a backbeat or a Latin pattern
How you know Jazz blues, bebop era, every recording The record, the style (“funk”, “Latin”, “even 8ths”)

The point is that the notation is identical. Everything that separates these two tunes in performance comes from outside the notes: the style, the era, the recording and the band.

6. Reading a new lead sheet

When you open a chart you have not played before, before you play a note:

  1. Look at the top of the page for a style or feel word, a ♫ = ♩ ♪³ sign, or “even 8ths”.
  2. Look at the tempo. The faster it is, the straighter the swing.
  3. Know where the tune comes from. A jazz standard or a bebop blues swings unless told otherwise. A funk, Latin, rock, soul or bossa nova tune does not.
  4. Listen to a recording. It is the only thing that settles the question, and it tells you about the accents and the note lengths too, which no lead sheet shows.
  5. Listen to the band. If the drummer plays the swing ride pattern, match its ratio; if the drummer plays straight eighths on the hi-hat, play straight. The ratio is shared, not chosen alone.

Then practise both tunes in this lesson at three tempos each, and play the slider settings from the tables until you can hear the difference without looking.
